Search words: SI, metric, prefixes, dimensional analysis, significant figures, uncertainty, conversion.

children.note: A number without a unit says nothing: "the bridge is 40" could be metres or feet. Engineers in Kenya and nearly everywhere use SI, so a drawing from Nairobi reads the same in Mombasa or Mumbai.

children.topic: A quantity is defined by how it is measured
children.note: Length by a rule, time by a clock; speed is then calculated as distance over time. Define it by the method of measuring or by the formula from other measurements.

manas.q: How is a physical quantity defined?

children.topic: Two systems: SI and English units
children.note: SI (metric) is used by almost every country and by all of science. English (imperial) units — feet, pounds, miles — survive mainly in the USA. You will meet inch-based bolts ("SAE") on imported machines.

children.topic: SI is coordinated by the BIPM in Paris
children.note: The International Bureau of Weights and Measures keeps the definitions; since 2019 every base unit is fixed by a constant of nature, not by a metal object.

manas.q: Since 2019, what are SI base units defined by?

children.note: Everything measurable is built from seven base quantities. Learn the unit and its symbol: m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd. Symbols are case-sensitive: "K" is kelvin, "k" is kilo.

manas.q: Name the seven SI base units with their symbols.

children.note: Since 1983: how far light goes through empty space in 1/299 792 458 s. That fixes the speed of light at exactly 299 792 458 m/s — the constant defines the unit.

manas.q: How is the metre defined, and what number does that fix exactly?

children.note: Until 2019 a platinum–iridium cylinder near Paris, which slowly lost about 50 micrograms. Now fixed through the Planck constant and measured on a Kibble balance. The only base unit whose name carries a prefix.

manas.q: What replaced the metal cylinder as the definition of the kilogram?

children.note: Since 1967: the time for 9 192 631 770 vibrations of a caesium atom. GPS and M-Pesa timestamps depend on clocks this exact.

manas.q: What does the second count?

children.note: The base unit for electricity; charge (coulomb) is current × time, so 1 C = 1 A·s.
Thermodynamic temperature; 0 K is absolute zero. A kelvin step equals a Celsius step, and 0 °C = 273.15 K. Write "K", never "°K".

manas.q: Convert 25 °C to kelvin.

children.note: Counts particles (about 6.022 × 10²³ of them). Chemistry and materials courses use it constantly.
Brightness as the eye sees it; used in lighting design. Rare in first-year mechanics.
Multiply or divide base units and you get every other unit. 22 derived units have special names (newton, pascal, joule, watt…); each can still be written in base units.

manas.q: What is a derived unit? Give two examples.

children.note: Length × length and length × length × length. 1 litre is 10⁻³ m³ (a 10 cm cube), one of the non-SI units accepted with SI.

manas.q: How many cubic metres is one litre?

children.note: Distance over time, and change of speed over time. A car at 60 km/h is moving at about 16.7 m/s.
Mass per volume. Water is about 1000 kg/m³, the same as 1 g/cm³: 1000 kg = 10⁶ g spread over 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³. Steel is about 7850 kg/m³.

manas.q: What is the density of water in kg/m³?

children.note: From F = ma: one newton accelerates one kilogram at one metre per second squared. A 1 kg bag of sugar weighs about 9.8 N on Earth.

manas.q: Write the newton in base units.

children.note: Force spread over an area. Atmospheric pressure is about 101 kPa; a car tyre about 220 kPa above that.
Work = force × distance. Lifting that 1 kg bag by 1 m takes about 9.8 J. 1 kWh of electricity is 3.6 MJ.

manas.q: How many joules in one kilowatt-hour?

children.note: Energy per second. A 2 kW kettle uses 2000 J every second; a 100 W solar panel at full sun gives 100 J each second.
Angle = arc length ÷ radius, so metres cancel. Trig functions in physics formulas expect radians.
Degrees Celsius, litres and electron-volts are allowed but always convertible: °C = K − 273.15, 1 L = 10⁻³ m³, 1 t (tonne) = 1000 kg = 1 Mg.
One unit covers every scale by adding a power-of-ten prefix: nanometres in a chip, kilometres on a road. Memorise the common ones; the full table is on the OpenStax page.

manas.q: What do kilo, mega, giga, milli, micro and nano mean as powers of ten?

children.note: kilo, mega, giga, tera. A 5 GW power station; a 2 TB disk. Capital letters from mega upward.
milli, micro, nano, pico. A 3 mm bolt; a 10 µF capacitor; a 500 nm wavelength.
centi, deci, hecto, deka — common in everyday life (cm, dL, hectare = 100 m × 100 m) but engineers prefer steps of 1000.
No "megagigametre". For mass the prefix goes on the gram, not the kilogram: 1000 kg is 1 Mg (one megagram), also called a tonne.

manas.q: What is 1000 kg written with a single prefix?

children.note: Step 1: kg → g by × 10³, giving 1.93 × 10¹⁶ g. Step 2: the nearest prefixes are peta (10¹⁵) and exa (10¹⁸). Step 3: 10¹⁶ = 10 × 10¹⁵, so 19.3 Pg (petagrams) — a number between 1 and 1000.

manas.q: Express 1.93 × 10¹³ kg using one prefix so the number is between 1 and 1000.

children.note: Also correct, but the convention is a number between 1 and 1000 so the value reads naturally. Both are the same mass.

Multiply by a conversion factor — a fraction equal to one, such as (1 km / 1000 m) — arranged so the unwanted unit cancels. Write the units in every line; if they do not cancel, the fraction is upside down.

manas.q: What is a conversion factor and how do you know which way up to write it?

children.note: Multiply by (1 km per 1000 m): the metres cancel and 80 m becomes 0.080 km. Same answer by prefix: 8.0 × 10¹ m with kilo = 10³ gives 8.0 × 10⁻² km.
60 km/h × (1000 m / 1 km) × (1 h / 3600 s) = 16.7 m/s. Quick rule: divide km/h by 3.6.

manas.q: Convert 90 km/h to m/s.

children.topic: Worked: 10 miles in 20 minutes, in m/s
children.note: First in the given units: half a mile per minute. Then two factors — 1609 m per mile and one minute per 60 s — give 13 m/s. Two factors, two cancellations.
5 L × (10⁻³ m³ / 1 L) = 5 × 10⁻³ m³ = 0.005 m³. Mass of that water ≈ 1000 kg/m³ × 0.005 m³ = 5 kg.

manas.q: A 20-litre jerrycan of water: volume in m³ and mass in kg?

children.topic: Squared and cubed units need the factor twice or thrice
children.note: 1 m² = (100 cm)² = 10 000 cm²; 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³. Forgetting the power is the classic error in area and volume conversions.

manas.q: How many cm³ in 1 m³?

children.note: A walking speed of 1.4 m/s or a car at 25 m/s is believable; 1400 m/s is not. If the size is wrong by a thousand, a prefix was probably missed.

Every quantity has a dimension built from L (length), M (mass), T (time), I (current), Θ (temperature), N (amount) and J (light). Square brackets mean "dimension of": [v] = LT⁻¹. Dimensions obey algebra like units.

manas.q: What are the seven dimension symbols?

children.note: You can only add, subtract or equate quantities with the same dimension — no apples plus oranges. Both sides of an equation must agree.

manas.q: State the two rules of dimensional consistency.

children.topic: Rule 2: sin, cos, log, exp take pure numbers
children.note: Their arguments must be dimensionless, and their outputs are dimensionless too. sin(at²/s) is fine because LT⁻²·T²/L = 1.
All seven powers zero — a pure number. Angles in radians, ratios, π, 2, efficiency, strain.

children.topic: Worked: πr² or 2πr for the area of a circle?
children.note: [πr²] = 1·L² = L², the dimension of area. [2πr] = L, a length — so it is the circumference. Dimensions pick the right form but not the constant (they cannot tell πr² from 2πr²).

manas.q: Use dimensions to decide which of 4πr² and 4πr³/3 is the volume of a sphere.

children.topic: Worked: is s = vt + ½at² consistent?
children.note: [s] = L. [vt] = LT⁻¹·T = L. [½at²] = LT⁻²·T² = L. All three terms are lengths, so yes. Swap to s = vt² + ½at and the terms become LT and LT⁻¹ — nonsense.

manas.q: Check s = vt² + ½at for dimensional consistency.

children.topic: Uses: catch typos, rebuild forgotten formulas
children.note: A quick dimension check finds algebra slips before the calculator does. It also suggests how a new quantity must depend on others — a tool you will use in fluids (Reynolds number).
Dimensional analysis never finds a dimensionless factor such as ½ or 2π. Those come from the physics.
Measurements are never exact. Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is how closely repeats agree. A reported number should show only the digits you actually know.

manas.q: Explain the difference between accuracy and precision.

children.topic: Accurate vs precise: the GPS target picture
children.note: Dots spread wide but centred on the target: accurate, not precise. Dots tightly grouped but off-centre: precise, not accurate. A good instrument is both.
A length 2.00 m ± 0.02 m means the true value probably lies between 1.98 and 2.02 m. Percent uncertainty = δA/A × 100 % = 1 %.

manas.q: A mass is 5.0 kg ± 0.1 kg. What is the percent uncertainty?

children.topic: Multiplying or dividing: add percent uncertainties
children.note: Area of a 2.00 m ± 1 % by 1.50 m ± 2 % panel: 3.00 m² ± 3 %, i.e. ± 0.09 m².

children.topic: Significant figures: the digits you trust
children.note: 36.7 cm has three; 0.0025 m has two (leading zeros do not count); 1200 is ambiguous — write 1.2 × 10³ or 1.200 × 10³ to say what you mean.

manas.q: How many significant figures in 0.0025 and in 36.70?

children.topic: Multiplication and division: fewest sig figs wins
children.note: 2.3 m × 1.457 m = 3.4 m² (two figures, because 2.3 has only two).

children.topic: Addition and subtraction: fewest decimal places wins
children.note: 12.4 m + 0.057 m = 12.5 m (one decimal place, set by 12.4).

manas.q: 12.4 + 0.057 to the correct number of figures?

children.note: 9.8 m/s² × 5.0 kg = 49 N, not 49.000. Extra digits claim a precision you never measured.
The gap between your result and the accepted value. If it is bigger than your uncertainty, look for a systematic error (a mis-zeroed scale, a stretched tape).
Engineers estimate before they calculate — to size a pump, a budget, a tank — then check the detailed answer against the estimate. Aim for the right power of ten, not the last digit.

children.topic: Method: break it into things you know
children.note: Water for a 50-house estate: 50 houses × 5 people × 100 L/day ≈ 25 000 L/day = 25 m³/day. Each factor is a rough guess; the product is usually within a factor of 2–3.

manas.q: Estimate the daily water need of a 50-house estate and state your assumptions.

children.note: Write the answer as 10ⁿ: 25 m³ is "of order 10 m³". Two estimates that differ by a factor of 3 are the same order of magnitude.

children.topic: Check limits and units at the end
children.note: Does the estimate have the right unit? Does it grow the right way when one input grows? A per-day figure that is far above a river's flow is a sign something is wrong.
The errors first-years make most often — each one has cost marks or, in practice, money.

children.topic: Mixing km/h with m/s in one formula
children.note: Convert everything to base SI before you substitute. v = 60 into s = vt with t in seconds gives nonsense.

children.topic: Forgetting to square the factor for areas
children.note: 1 m² is 10 000 cm², not 100. Why: a square 1 m on each side is 100 cm by 100 cm, and area multiplies both sides, so the factor 100 is used twice. Check: picture a 1 km² plot as 1000 m × 1000 m = 10⁶ m².
The kilogram already has a prefix; 1000 kg is 1 Mg or 1 t.

children.topic: Degrees in a trig function expecting radians
children.note: Formulas such as ω = θ/t or arc = rθ need radians. Set the calculator mode before you start.
Round to the significant figures the data allow; keep extra digits only in the middle of a calculation.

children.topic: Writing units in the wrong case
children.note: kg not KG, m not M (M is mega), s not S (S is siemens), K not °K. The symbol is the unit's identity.
Say the answer aloud, then tap the bubble to check against the source page. Five questions, no calculator needed for most.

children.topic: Q1 · Write the pascal and the joule in base units
children.note: Pa = N/m² = kg·m⁻¹·s⁻². J = N·m = kg·m²·s⁻².

manas.q: Write the pascal and the joule in SI base units.
Convert 72 km/h to m/s.

children.topic: Q3 · Is F = mv²/r dimensionally a force?
children.note: [mv²/r] = M·L²T⁻²/L = MLT⁻², the same as [ma]. Yes.

manas.q: Show that mv²/r has the dimensions of force.

children.note: 4.7 × 10⁻⁶ m = 4.7 µm. Why: the decimal point moves 6 places to reach 4.7, and 10⁻⁶ is the prefix micro (µ). Check: 4.7 µm × 10⁻⁶ gives back 0.000 004 7 m; that is a bit smaller than a red blood cell.

manas.q: Express 0.0000047 m with a metric prefix.

children.topic: Q5 · A tape reads 3.21 m ± 0.01 m. Percent uncertainty?
children.note: 0.01 / 3.21 × 100 % ≈ 0.3 %. Why: percent uncertainty is the ± amount divided by the reading, so it shows how good the measurement is whatever its size. Check: 0.3 % of 3.21 m is about 0.01 m, the ± we started with.

manas.q: A tape reads 3.21 m ± 0.01 m. What is the percent uncertainty?

children.note: Measure in SI, carry the units through every line, check dimensions before trusting a formula, and report only the digits you know. These four habits catch most engineering errors before they leave the desk.
Next map in this library: Statics — forces, free-body diagrams and equilibrium, where these units (N, N·m) go to work. Medicine and Soil Life libraries use the same SI prefixes.

nodeData.note: Forces, displacements and velocities have a size and a direction. Split them into parts, add them, multiply them — the maths behind statics and dynamics. Own-words notes from OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1 ch. 2 and Wikipedia; examples recomputed. Search words: vector, scalar, components, resultant, SOH CAH TOA, sine rule, cosine rule, dot product, cross product, unit vector, radian.

children.note: A scalar is just a size with a unit: 20 kg, 30 °C, 5 s. A vector also needs a direction: 20 N downward, 3 km east. If turning the arrow changes the answer, the quantity is a vector.

manas.q: What is the difference between a scalar and a vector?

children.note: Mass, time, temperature, energy, speed, distance. Adding them is ordinary arithmetic: 2 kg of sugar plus 3 kg is 5 kg.
Displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, torque, momentum. Two 3 N forces can add to anything from 0 N (opposite) to 6 N (same way).

manas.q: Two forces of 3 N act on a box. What range of totals is possible?

children.note: A matatu that goes from Kencom to Westlands and back has covered a distance but has zero displacement: displacement only cares where you ended up relative to where you started.

manas.q: A matatu drives a loop and returns to the stage. Its displacement?

children.note: Speed is how fast; velocity is how fast and which way. A car going round a roundabout at a steady 30 km/h has constant speed but changing velocity — so it is accelerating.
Bold letter (A), an arrow on top, or underlined in handwriting. The size alone (magnitude) is written A or |A|, always zero or positive.
Right-angled triangles turn a slanted vector into a horizontal part and a vertical part. Three ratios do almost all the work.
sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent. "Opposite" and "adjacent" are named from the angle you are using.

manas.q: State SOH CAH TOA.

children.note: In a right-angled triangle, hypotenuse² = side² + side². A 3 km east and 4 km north trip ends 5 km from the start.
sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹ give the angle back from a ratio. Why it matters: you usually know the components and want the direction.
A full turn is 360° or 2π rad, so 180° = π rad and 1 rad ≈ 57.3°. A radian is the angle where the arc length equals the radius. Rotation formulas (v = ωr) need radians.

manas.q: How many degrees in one radian?

children.note: Before any exam, type sin 30. If you get 0.5 you are in degrees; −0.988 means radians. Many lost marks come from the wrong mode, not wrong physics.

manas.q: Quick test that your calculator is in degree mode?

children.note: A road that rises 1 m for every 10 m along the level (10 % grade) is at tan⁻¹(0.1) = 5.7°. Small angles: the percent grade ÷ 100 is close to the angle in radians.

manas.q: What angle is a 10 % road gradient?

children.note: Any vector in a plane equals an x-part plus a y-part at right angles. Working in components turns hard geometry into two easy sums.

manas.q: Why do engineers split vectors into components?

children.note: For a vector of size A at angle θ above the +x axis: Aₓ = A cos θ, A_y = A sin θ. Check: Aₓ² + A_y² must give back A².

manas.q: Write the x- and y-components of a vector A at angle θ.

children.note: A rope pulls a cart with 500 N at 30° above the ground. Along the ground: 500 cos 30° = 433 N. Lifting part: 500 sin 30° = 250 N. Only the 433 N moves the cart forward.

manas.q: 500 N at 30° above horizontal: horizontal and vertical parts?

children.note: The 250 N upward part reduces how hard the cart presses on the ground, so it also reduces friction. Pulling a little upward can make a heavy load easier to drag.
Arrows of length 1 along x, y and z. A vector is written A = Aₓ i + A_y j (+ A_z k). The numbers in front are the scalar components and can be negative.
If a vector starts at (x₁, y₁) and ends at (x₂, y₂), its components are x₂ − x₁ and y₂ − y₁: end minus start, never the other way.

manas.q: A vector runs from (6, 1.6) to (2, 4.5). Its components?

children.topic: Back from components: size and angle
children.note: Size A = √(Aₓ² + A_y²). Direction tan θ = A_y ÷ Aₓ, measured anticlockwise from +x.
tan⁻¹ only returns −90° to +90°. For a vector with a negative x-part, add 180°. Example: (−4.0, 2.9) gives tan⁻¹ = −35.9°, but the true direction is 144.1°.

manas.q: Vector (−4.0, 2.9): the calculator says −35.9°. True direction?

children.note: Sketch it first. A vector pointing left and up must be between 90° and 180°; if the answer is not there, fix the quadrant.
Size and angle (A, θ) are polar coordinates; (Aₓ, A_y) are Cartesian. Same vector, two descriptions — convert with cos/sin one way and Pythagoras/tan the other.
The total of several vectors is called the resultant. Add by drawing (tip to tail) or, more accurately, by adding components.

manas.q: What is a resultant?

children.note: Draw the first arrow, start the second at its tip, and so on. The resultant runs from the first tail to the last tip. The order does not change the answer.
Put two vectors tail to tail and complete the parallelogram; the diagonal from the shared tail is their sum. Same answer as tip to tail.
Add all the x-parts, add all the y-parts, then rebuild size and angle. Works for any number of vectors and needs no scale drawing.

manas.q: Describe the component method for adding vectors.

children.topic: Worked: two forces on a hook

manas.q: 300 N at 0° plus 400 N at 60°: size and direction of the resultant?

children.note: The triangle formed has the angle 120° between the two sides: R² = 300² + 400² − 2·300·400·cos 120° = 370 000, so R = 608 N. Two methods agree.
sin φ ÷ 400 = sin 120° ÷ 608 gives φ = 34.7°, the same angle from +x.
A matatu goes 3.0 km east then 4.0 km north. Displacement: √(3² + 4²) = 5.0 km at tan⁻¹(4/3) = 53° north of east. The road distance is 7.0 km.

manas.q: 3.0 km east then 4.0 km north: displacement?

children.note: Fuel and fares depend on distance (7 km); a drone flying straight only needs the displacement (5 km).
A − B means A + (−B): flip B round and add it. Used for change in velocity, Δv = v_final − v_initial.
3A is three times as long, same direction. −A is the same length pointing the opposite way. Dividing a vector by its own size gives the unit vector of its direction.
For A = 3i + 4j, size 5, the unit vector is 0.6i + 0.8j. Multiply it by any size to get a vector that way.

manas.q: Unit vector in the direction of 3i + 4j?

children.note: For triangles without a right angle — truss members, cable pairs, survey lines.
c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C, where C is the angle opposite side c. When C = 90° it becomes Pythagoras. Use it when you know two sides and the angle between them.

manas.q: State the cosine rule. When does it reduce to Pythagoras?

children.note: a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B = c ÷ sin C. Use it when you know a side and the angle opposite it, plus one more piece.

manas.q: State the sine rule.

children.note: Given two sides and a non-included angle, the sine rule can give two possible triangles (sin x = sin(180° − x)). Sketch to decide which one is real.
If the angle between two force arrows (tail to tail) is θ, the triangle angle opposite the resultant is 180° − θ. So R² = a² + b² + 2ab cos θ. Mixing these two angles is a common error.

manas.q: Two forces with angle θ between them: resultant squared by cosine rule?

children.note: A · B = AB cos φ, where φ is the angle between them. The result is a scalar. It measures how much one vector points along the other.

manas.q: What is the dot product and is its result a scalar or a vector?

children.note: A · B = AₓBₓ + A_yB_y + A_zB_z. Because i · i = 1 and i · j = 0.

children.topic: Finding the angle between two vectors

manas.q: Angle between (3, 4) and (4, 3)?

children.note: If A · B = 0 (and neither is zero), they are at 90°. Quick check that a normal force is really perpendicular to a slope.

manas.q: What does a zero dot product tell you?

children.topic: Use: work done by a force
children.note: Work = F · d. A 50 N pull at 60° to the ground over 10 m does 50 × 10 × cos 60° = 250 J — only the part of the force along the motion counts.

manas.q: 50 N at 60° to the motion, 10 m: work done?

children.topic: Why a carried bag does no work horizontally
children.note: Your upward hold is at 90° to the walk, so cos 90° = 0. You get tired from muscles, but the force does no work on the bag along the road.
The part of A along a direction with unit vector u is A · u. Example: weight along a slope.
A × B is a vector at right angles to both, of size AB sin φ. It gives torque and the force on a current in a magnetic field.

manas.q: What is the size and direction of A × B?

children.note: Point the fingers of your right hand along A, curl them toward B; the thumb points along A × B. Order matters: B × A is the opposite direction.

manas.q: Is A × B equal to B × A?

children.note: i × j = k, j × k = i, k × i = j (go round in order); reversing the order gives a minus sign. Any vector crossed with itself is zero.
τ = r × F, size rF sin φ. 80 N at the end of a 0.25 m spanner, at right angles: 20 N·m. At 60° to the handle: 20 × sin 60° = 17.3 N·m.

manas.q: 80 N on a 0.25 m spanner at 60° to the handle: torque?

children.note: sin φ is largest (1) at 90°. Pushing along the handle (φ = 0) turns nothing — the same lever-arm idea as the statics map.
AB sin φ is the area of the parallelogram the two vectors make. Used later for areas and flux.
Choose axes along and across the slope — the motion is along it, so one component equation becomes simple.

children.topic: Weight on a slope at angle θ
children.note: Along the slope: mg sin θ (pulls it down the slope). Into the slope: mg cos θ (pressed into the surface, balanced by the normal force).

manas.q: Weight components along and into a slope at θ?

children.topic: Worked: loaded matatu on a 10 % grade
children.note: Mass 1500 kg, weight 14 700 N, angle 5.7°. Down-slope part: 14 700 × sin 5.7° ≈ 1460 N. The engine must supply this extra force just to hold speed uphill.

manas.q: 1500 kg vehicle on a 10 % grade: weight component down the slope?

children.note: sin θ ≈ 0.1 for a 10 % grade, so about one tenth of the weight: 1470 N. Close to the exact answer.
The angle between the weight and the "into the slope" axis equals the slope angle θ. Draw a steep slope to test: as θ → 90°, the down-slope part should become the whole weight (sin 90° = 1).
These cost marks in first-year tests.
3 N + 4 N is 7 N only if they point the same way; at right angles it is 5 N. Always add components.
Cos goes with the side next to the angle you use. If the angle is measured from the vertical, the horizontal part uses sin.

manas.q: A force makes angle α with the vertical. Horizontal part?

children.note: Check the signs of the components and sketch. Add 180° when x is negative.
sin 30 should be 0.5. Set degree mode, or convert.
A component pointing left or down is negative. Lose the sign and a force that should cancel will double instead.
Dot gives a number (work, projection); cross gives a vector (torque). Dot uses cos, cross uses sin.

manas.q: Which product gives torque, and which gives work?

children.note: Say the answer aloud; tap a bubble for the source page.

children.topic: Q1 · 200 N at 40° above horizontal: parts?

manas.q: 200 N at 40° above horizontal: horizontal and vertical parts?
Add (2i + 5j) N and (4i − 3j) N. Size?

children.note: Dot product 2 − 2 = 0, so yes.

manas.q: Are (2, −1) and (1, 2) perpendicular?

children.note: π/2 ≈ 1.571 rad and π/4 ≈ 0.785 rad. Multiply degrees by π/180.

manas.q: Convert 45° to radians.

children.topic: Q5 · Two 100 N forces 120° apart: resultant?
children.note: R² = 100² + 100² + 2·100·100·cos 120° = 10 000, so R = 100 N, pointing midway between them.

manas.q: Two 100 N forces 120° apart: resultant size?

children.note: Sketch, choose axes, split every vector into components with sin and cos, add the x-parts and the y-parts, then rebuild the size and angle — checking the quadrant. Dot gives "how much along"; cross gives "how much turning".
Earlier maps: Units, dimensions and estimation; Statics (ΣF = 0 is a vector sum; torque is a cross product). Next: Dynamics — Newton's second law uses the same components.
